prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Boeing is asking pilots who fly its 737 jets to pay careful attention to flight instruments after Dutch investigators said a faulty altimeter contributed to the recent crash of a 737 in the Netherlands. Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 broke into three pieces near Schiphol Airport on February 25. The 737 is the most widely flown jet in commercial aviation. More than 6,000 have been sold, according to Boeing. "Boeing reminds all operators to make sure flight crews pay close attention to all primary flight controls during critical stages of a flight," Boeing spokesman Jim Proulx told CNN on Thursday. On February 25, Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 from Istanbul to Amsterdam dropped from the sky on approach to the landing strip at Schiphol Airport, breaking into three pieces in a muddy field. Nine people died and 80 people were hurt in the accident. In a memo to pilots, Boeing says there was a malfunction in one of the plane's two altimeters, which measure the altitude above the terrain where the plane is going to land. The left altimeter was giving "erroneous" information, indicating that the plane was below 7 or 8 feet from ground level when it was actually about 2,000 feet in the air, the memo said. That caused the automatic throttles to slow the plane down. "Boeing recommends operators inform flight crews of the above investigation details and the (Dutch Safety Board) interim report when it is released. In addition, crews should be reminded to carefully monitor primary flight instruments," the memo said. The plane was on automatic pilot when it crashed, said Pieter van Vollenhoven, head of the Dutch Safety Board. The weather was misty at the time of the crash, possibly keeping the pilots from noticing their altitude, Van Vollenhoven said. Automatic pilot should not be used for landings if altimeters are malfunctioning, he said. Dutch investigators said there had been faulty meter readings on two other flights of the same jet, but the pilots were able to land. In the Amsterdam crash, the pilots did not recognize the altimeter problem until it was too late, Van Vollenhoven said. The Boeing memo notes that "the autothrottle, which uses the left radio altimeter data, transitioned to landing flare mode and retarded the throttles to the idle stop. The throttles remained at the idle stop for approximately 100 seconds during which time the airspeed decreased to approximately 40 knots below the selected approach speed." Proulx said he did not know what that speed was for that particular 737 model. The warning issued by Boeing was for many other models of 737 jets, not just the 737-800 involved in the Amsterdam crash.

(CNN) — Following findings by Dutch investigators that a defective altitude gauge played a role in the recent crash of a 737 in the Netherlands, Boeing has urged pilots operating its 737 aircraft to closely watch their flight instruments.

Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 crashed near Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport on February 25, splitting into three sections. The 737 is commercial aviation’s most commonly operated jet, with more than 6,000 sold, according to Boeing.

Boeing spokesman Jim Proulx told CNN on Thursday that the company was reminding every operator to ensure crews carefully observe all primary flight controls during crucial portions of a flight.

Flight 1951, traveling from Istanbul to Amsterdam, fell during its approach to Schiphol’s runway and came down in a muddy field. Nine people were killed and 80 others were injured.

In a notice sent to pilots, Boeing said one of the aircraft’s two altimeters—which determine the plane’s height above the ground in the landing area—had failed. According to the notice, the left altimeter incorrectly showed the jet as being less than 7 or 8 feet above the ground when it was actually flying at roughly 2,000 feet. The false reading prompted the autothrottle system to reduce the aircraft’s speed.

The memo advised airlines to brief flight crews on the known details of the investigation and on the Dutch Safety Board’s preliminary report once it became available. It also called for pilots to be reminded to monitor their primary flight instruments closely.

Pieter van Vollenhoven, chairman of the Dutch Safety Board, said the aircraft was being flown on autopilot when it crashed. Misty conditions may have prevented the pilots from realizing their true altitude, he added. Van Vollenhoven said autopilot should not be used during landing when altitude instruments are not functioning properly.

Dutch investigators also found that the same aircraft had produced incorrect instrument readings on two earlier flights, although the pilots landed safely on both occasions. In the Amsterdam accident, Van Vollenhoven said, the crew identified the altimeter failure only after it was too late to recover.

Boeing’s notice explained that the autothrottle relied on information from the left radio altimeter. Because of the faulty data, the system entered landing-flare mode and moved the throttles back to the idle position. They stayed there for about 100 seconds, during which the aircraft’s airspeed dropped to approximately 40 knots below the speed selected for the approach.

Proulx said he did not know the designated approach speed for the specific 737 involved. Boeing’s alert applied to numerous versions of the 737, rather than only the 737-800 that crashed near Amsterdam.

**Boeing warns 737 pilots after faulty altimeter linked to Amsterdam crash**

**AMSTERDAM, Netherlands —** Boeing has warned pilots flying its 737 aircraft to closely monitor their flight instruments after investigators found that a faulty radio altimeter contributed to the crash of Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 near Amsterdam.

The Boeing 737-800 was approaching Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport on February 25, 2009, when it lost speed, stalled and crashed into a field short of the runway. Nine people were killed, including three pilots, and dozens were injured.

A preliminary investigation by the Dutch Safety Board found that one of the aircraft’s radio altimeters incorrectly indicated the plane was below ground level while it was still nearly 2,000 feet in the air. The false reading caused the automated thrust system to reduce engine power to idle, as if the aircraft were about to land.

The crew did not recognize the resulting loss of airspeed until it was too late to recover, investigators said.

In guidance sent to operators, Boeing urged pilots to compare radio-altimeter readings with other flight instruments during approach. If conflicting information appears, crews should disengage the autothrottle and control engine power manually, the company said.

Boeing emphasized that pilots must continue monitoring airspeed, altitude and engine thrust even when automated systems are engaged.

The warning did not order airlines to ground or immediately modify their aircraft. Dutch investigators continued examining the crash, including the performance of the altimeter, the aircraft’s automation and the crew’s response.

The Dutch Safety Board’s preliminary investigation found that Turkish Airlines Flight 1951, a Boeing 737-800, was descending toward Schiphol on February 25, 2009, when its left radio altimeter falsely indicated about **–8 feet**, although the aircraft was still roughly **1,950 feet above the ground**.

Because the autopilot and autothrottle were using that altimeter’s data, the autothrottle interpreted the aircraft as having landed and moved the thrust levers to idle in “retard” mode. The crew did not immediately notice the resulting loss of airspeed. When the stall warning activated, they attempted to add power and recover, but the aircraft was too low; it stalled and crashed short of the runway.

There were **135 people aboard**. **Nine were killed**, including members of the cockpit crew, and the preliminary reporting listed **86 people as injured**; later injury totals varied depending on classification.

Following the findings, Boeing advised 737 operators to watch for discrepancies between the two radio-altimeter readings, follow the relevant malfunction procedures, and **disengage the autothrottle and control thrust manually** if unreliable radio-altitude information affects the automatic flight systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed aviation news article explaining how erroneous radio-altimeter data caused a Boeing 737’s throttles to remain idle during its approach to Amsterdam.
counterfactuals.output:
# False height signal sent Boeing 737’s throttles to idle during Amsterdam approach

**AMSTERDAM —** A faulty radio-altimeter signal caused the automatic throttles of a Turkish Airlines Boeing 737-800 to reduce engine power to idle while the aircraft was still nearly 2,000 feet above the ground, setting in motion the loss of airspeed that preceded the jet’s crash short of Amsterdam Airport Schiphol.

Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 was approaching Schiphol’s Runway 18R on February 25, 2009, after a scheduled flight from Istanbul. The aircraft came down in a field about 1.5 kilometers, or roughly one mile, before the runway threshold. Nine of the 135 people aboard were killed, including the three pilots in the cockpit, and many others were injured.

The Dutch Safety Board’s investigation found that the engines and flight controls had not suffered a conventional mechanical failure. Instead, the accident centered on a false indication from the aircraft’s left radio altimeter and the way that erroneous information was used by the 737’s autothrottle system.

## A reading of minus eight feet

Radio altimeters measure an aircraft’s actual height above the terrain by transmitting radio signals toward the ground and timing their return. Unlike barometric altimeters, which indicate altitude based on air pressure, radio altimeters are intended to provide precise height information during the final stages of an approach and landing.

As Flight 1951 descended through approximately 1,950 feet, the left radio altimeter abruptly indicated **minus eight feet**. The aircraft was, in reality, still high above the ground.

That implausible reading had important consequences because the autothrottle channel controlling thrust was using the left radio-altimeter input. To the autothrottle logic, the aircraft appeared to have reached the final moments of the landing.

During a normal automatic landing sequence, the 737’s autothrottle enters **RETARD** mode close to the runway. It then moves the thrust levers toward idle so that the aircraft can touch down without carrying unnecessary engine power.

On Flight 1951, the false radio-altimeter value caused RETARD mode to activate prematurely. The thrust levers moved back and the engines settled at idle even though the aircraft was still on the approach, far above the runway.

The throttles were not mechanically jammed. The automation was commanding idle thrust, and the pilots could have overridden it by manually advancing the levers. But because the aircraft continued to follow the instrument approach and no immediate dramatic failure occurred, the developing energy loss was not recognized in time.

## Different systems received different pictures

A key feature of the accident was that the 737’s automation did not react as though the whole aircraft were eight feet below ground. Different systems were receiving or using different radio-altimeter information.

The autopilot continued attempting to maintain the glideslope, while the autothrottle behaved as though the aircraft were already at landing height. That produced a dangerous mismatch: the autopilot was still flying an airborne approach, but the thrust system had entered a mode intended for touchdown.

As engine power remained at idle, drag increased with the landing gear and flaps extended. Airspeed began to fall below the selected approach speed.

The autopilot responded in the way it was designed to respond to a loss of speed and lift while trying to remain on the glideslope: it progressively raised the nose. That pitch increase initially helped the aircraft hold its flight path, but it also increased the wing’s angle of attack and concealed the severity of the energy loss. The jet was maintaining the approach path by trading away airspeed.

This was not a self-correcting condition. With the thrust levers still at idle, the aircraft had no adequate source of energy to maintain both its speed and its descent profile.

## High workload and an unstable approach

The investigation also found that the approach was already demanding. Air traffic control had positioned the aircraft in a way that required the crew to intercept the glideslope from above, rather than establishing the jet below it in the usual manner.

The crew was therefore configuring the aircraft, completing checklists and attempting to stabilize the approach while monitoring the automatic systems. The faulty radio-altimeter indication was noticed, but its connection to the autothrottle’s RETARD mode and the idle thrust setting was not fully understood.

The aircraft did not meet the airline’s stabilized-approach criteria at the required height. A go-around should have been initiated, investigators said, but the approach was continued.

The flight crew’s attention was divided among the approach path, configuration changes, radio communications and the abnormal radio-altimeter indication. Meanwhile, the most fundamental warning sign—the continuing reduction in airspeed with the thrust levers at idle—was not acted upon soon enough.

## Stall warning came too late

As the 737 descended, its speed deteriorated significantly below the intended approach speed. The autopilot continued increasing pitch to remain near the glideslope until the wing approached a stall.

At about 460 feet above the ground, the control columns began to shake as the stick-shaker stall warning activated. The crew then attempted to recover by lowering the nose and applying power.

But the aircraft was already low, slow and close to the stall. Turbofan engines also require time to accelerate from idle to high thrust. With only seconds and a few hundred feet remaining, there was insufficient altitude to regain the lost airspeed and arrest the descent.

The aircraft struck the field short of the runway, breaking into several sections.

## More than a single faulty component

The Dutch Safety Board concluded that the radio-altimeter malfunction initiated the chain of events, but it did not treat the failed indication as the sole cause.

Investigators highlighted several interacting factors:

- The left radio altimeter supplied an erroneous height without the autothrottle rejecting the value as implausible.
- The autothrottle entered landing RETARD mode at a high altitude and commanded idle thrust.
- The automation architecture allowed the autopilot and autothrottle to operate on inconsistent assumptions.
- The crew did not adequately monitor airspeed and thrust.
- The abnormal indication was not recognized as a direct threat to the aircraft’s energy state.
- The approach remained unstable but was not discontinued.
- Stall recovery began too close to the ground to succeed.
- Previous radio-altimeter irregularities had not led to an effective, lasting correction.

The investigation also raised concerns about information available to operators and pilots. A radio-altimeter fault might appear to be an instrument problem affecting height callouts or landing displays, but on the 737 it could also influence automatic thrust and other systems. The broader operational consequences were not sufficiently apparent to crews and maintenance organizations, the board found.

## A lesson in automation monitoring

Flight 1951 became a prominent example of how one erroneous sensor can create an automation mode that is technically logical but completely inappropriate for the aircraft’s real situation.

The autothrottle did what it had been programmed to do when told the aircraft was at or below landing height: it retarded the thrust levers. The autopilot also continued doing what it had been programmed to do: hold the approach path. Together, however, those actions allowed airspeed to decay toward a stall.

The accident underscored that automatic systems do not necessarily share a single, consistent understanding of the aircraft’s condition. Multiple computers may use different sensor sources, and a plausible signal to one system can trigger a hazardous response even when another system continues operating normally.

Investigators emphasized that pilots must monitor the aircraft’s basic energy state—particularly airspeed, pitch and thrust—regardless of which automatic modes are engaged. On an approach, unexplained idle thrust, falling speed or a persistent automation anomaly should prompt immediate intervention and, if necessary, a go-around.

In the case of Flight 1951, the decisive failure was not that the engines could not produce power. It was that bad height data convinced the autothrottle that the landing was already under way, leaving the engines at idle until the aircraft no longer had enough altitude or airspeed to recover.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Boeing’s memo to 737 operators following the crash of Turkish Airlines Flight 1951, using quotes from Boeing spokesman Jim Proulx and Dutch investigator Pieter van Vollenhoven.
counterfactuals.output:
Boeing sent a memo to operators of its 737 aircraft after preliminary findings linked the crash of Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 to a faulty radio altimeter.

The Turkish Airlines 737-800 crashed short of Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport on Feb. 25, 2009, killing nine people. Dutch investigators found that, during the approach, the captain’s radio altimeter abruptly indicated the aircraft was below ground level. That false reading caused the autothrottle system to reduce engine power to idle, allowing the aircraft’s speed to decay until it stalled.

Dutch Safety Board chairman Pieter van Vollenhoven said the altimeter “suddenly indicated a change in altitude — from 1,950 feet to minus 8 feet — and passed this on to the automatic throttle.” He added that “when the crew noticed this, it was too late to take action.”

Boeing’s Multi-Operator Message did not order a redesign or grounding. Instead, it reminded 737 crews to compare radio-altimeter readings and closely monitor airspeed, altitude and engine power during approach, particularly when using the autopilot and autothrottle.

Boeing spokesman Jim Proulx described the communication as reinforcing existing instructions: “It re-emphasizes the procedures that already exist for flight crews to follow.” The memo advised crews to disengage automatic systems and use appropriate manual procedures if the two radio altimeters disagree or other flight instruments show an abnormal condition.

Investigators emphasized that the defective altimeter alone did not make the crash inevitable; the accident resulted from the interaction between the bad reading, the automated throttle response and the crew’s delayed recognition of the falling airspeed.

# BREAKING: Faulty altitude reading, autopilot response emerge as focus in Schiphol 737 crash

**AMSTERDAM —** Investigators examining the Turkish Airlines Boeing 737-800 that crashed short of Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport say a faulty radio-altimeter reading caused the aircraft’s automated throttle system to reduce engine power during the final approach.

The jet, operating as Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 from Istanbul, came down in a field near the runway, killing nine people and injuring dozens.

Preliminary findings indicate that the left radio altimeter suddenly showed the aircraft was at or below ground level while it was still hundreds of metres above the airport. With the autopilot and autothrottle engaged, the aircraft’s systems interpreted the false reading as a signal that the plane was about to land. The autothrottle pulled the engines back to idle, allowing the 737 to lose speed.

The autopilot continued guiding the aircraft toward the runway, but it did not restore sufficient power as the airspeed fell. The crew attempted to recover after stall warnings activated, investigators said, but the aircraft was too low.

Misty weather and low cloud meant the pilots were conducting an instrument approach and had fewer outside visual cues that the aircraft was slowing. Investigators have not identified the weather as the direct cause, but it may have increased the crew’s reliance on automated systems and cockpit instruments.

The radio-altimeter problem was not unprecedented. Investigators said the same system had produced implausible readings on earlier flights, raising questions about whether the recurring fault had been properly reported, diagnosed and repaired.

Boeing has since issued a warning to operators of several next-generation 737 variants, including the 737-600, -700, -800 and -900. The notice advises crews to closely monitor radio-altimeter indications and to disengage the autothrottle and associated automatic landing functions if altitude readings become unreliable.

The findings remain preliminary. Investigators are continuing to examine the aircraft’s maintenance history, cockpit procedures, crew response and the design of the automation to determine why the false reading was allowed to develop into a fatal stall.
